T2.6 APPARATUS NOW EXISTS (2026-08-17): scripts/reproducible-build.sh, and all SEVEN release targets build byte-identically from two independent trees. THE BUILD WAS NOT REPRODUCIBLE BEFORE: -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w' is not enough, because Go stamps vcs=git / vcs.revision / vcs.time / vcs.modified and a commit-derived module version into every binary, so the same source built inside the repo and from a tarball produced DIFFERENT BYTES. -buildvcs=false removes all five. Easy to miss because vcs.time is the COMMIT time, not the build time, so two builds of one commit already matched; the divergence appears only when a .git directory does -- i.e. CI-from-checkout vs user-from-tarball, the case that matters. All three build sites now share identical flags, so a node building from source gets byte-identical output to the published release, and an audit fails the build if any drifts (that audit was itself found VACUOUS first: it matched the flag inside the comment explaining the flag). T2.6 STILL NOT CLAIMED -- one machine, one toolchain, one GOAMD64 level; 'independently built' needs a second machine, and E13.1's three-platform half needs CI. E2.2 still needs a controlled-RTT link. ASN diversity still degrades to prefix-only for IPv4 (go-libp2p-asn-util is IPv6-only). F3 CLOSED 2026-08-17 (PCP, RFC 6887): internal/axon/peer/pcp.go, 10 tests, five injections verified. THE ENUM WAS LYING -- the roadmap correctly said PCP is not implemented, but a single MappingNATPMP constant was commented 'NAT-PMP / PCP' and stringified 'nat-pmp'. Those are TWO PROTOCOLS, RFC 6886 and RFC 6887, sharing UDP port 5351 and a lineage and nothing else; a gateway answering one need not answer the other, so an operator reading a log could not tell which had been spoken and the roadmap could describe PCP as covered by a constant that never implemented it. WHY PCP: NAT-PMP has no IPv6, no way to request a specific external address, and NO MAPPING NONCE, so it cannot distinguish its own response from an off-path forgery, and cannot survive the CGNAT a large share of residential and every mobile network now runs. THE NONCE IS A SECURITY PROPERTY: RFC 6887 11.1 requires a random 96-bit nonce echoed in the response; without it an off-path attacker spraying UDP at 5351 convinces this node it holds a mapping on an external address THE ATTACKER CHOSE, and the reachability machine then advertises it. Drawn ONCE PER MAPPER because it identifies the MAPPING -- a refresh with a fresh nonce creates a SECOND mapping instead of extending the first, leaking one per cycle until the gateway is full. THE GRANTED LEASE IS THE GATEWAY'S not the one asked for (11.2): refreshing on the requested figure refreshes AFTER the mapping has already expired, which looks exactly like a working mapping right up until it is not. GATEWAY-RESTART DETECTION (8.5): a restarted gateway has lost every mapping but keeps answering, because the response is generated from the request, and the state machine demotes on a FAILED refresh -- so a backwards epoch is an error. ADDRESS_MISMATCH (code 12) is named loudly: a second layer of NAT, so no mapping here can make the node reachable. PCP is tried BEFORE NAT-PMP per RFC 6887 16. TWO THINGS FOUND ON THE WAY: (1) MappingConfig.protocols() was DEAD CONFIG -- it returned a preference order and nothing turned it into mappers, so adding PCP would have implemented a protocol nothing could reach; NewMappersFor now does, and re-checks the opt-in because UPnP discovery broadcasts on the local network. (2) defaultGateway DID NOT EXIST -- NewNATPMPMapper took a gateway nobody supplied; it now reads /proc/net/route rather than assuming the .1 of the local /24, and ON THE MACHINE THIS WAS WRITTEN ON THE GATEWAY IS 192.168.1.254, so the guess would have been wrong here, and a wrong guess sends mapping requests to an unrelated host that never consented to one. STILL OPEN and NOT F3's: nothing in cmd/ calls NewMappersFor or NewMappingManager -- port mapping is now CONSTRUCTIBLE, not WIRED. CASE 1 VERIFIED: a link survived an initiator address change onto a new UDP socket. CASE 2 VERIFIED AS A REFUSAL: AddPath returns 'server cannot initiate connection migration', so the analysis that inbound links die rests on a library property and not on prose. THE RACE DETECTOR WAS NOT ACTUALLY RUNNING, FOUND 2026-08-21, and eleven notes in this file say 'race-clean'. `go test -race` needs cgo and cgo needs a C compiler, which is absent from the environment this tree is currently built in -- so every run here had been CGO_ENABLED=0, and -race silently was not part of it. WITH A COMPILER SUPPLIED, internal/axon/peer FAILED with 24 DATA RACE reports across 5 tests. NOT IN PRODUCTION CODE: the racing party is fakeGateway in pcp_test.go, a UDP test harness whose serve() goroutine reads eight knobs on every request while the tests write them between requests, and which writes lastRequest while the tests read it. THE COST WAS NOT THE HARNESS, IT WAS THE COVERAGE: a package that cannot be run under -race cannot be checked under -race AT ALL, so any real race in the peerbook, the annotator or the containment list added this week was hidden behind this file's noise. That is the same shape as the vacuous telemetry guard and the collection error -- a check that reads as coverage while covering nothing. FIXED by putting a mutex on the harness, taking ONE SNAPSHOT of the knobs per request (so a knob changed mid-response cannot produce a reply that is half one setting and half another), and giving the tests a set() closure and a request() accessor. THE WHOLE TREE IS NOW VERIFIED RACE-CLEAN FOR REAL: go test -race ./... over 48 packages, exit 0, zero DATA RACE reports. The eleven claims are true; nothing here had been checking them. AND WITH -race FINALLY RUNNING, A SELF-REVIEW OF THIS WEEK'S NEW CODE FOUND TWO REAL RACES IN IT, 2026-08-21 (the 6.3 adversarial pass, turned on my own work). Both were invisible until a test actually exercised the concurrency, which no existing test did. (1) reputation.Reducer.Reduce captured the inner per-issuer map under RLock and then ITERATED IT AFTER RELEASING THE LOCK -- twice -- while Accept writes that same map under Lock: a concurrent read/write, and a 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic under load. Fixed by snapshotting the map under the lock and iterating the copy. TestReduceRaceAgainstAccept reproduces it. (2) path.Source.Candidates wrote its s.last sidecar report with NO lock, and Selector.SelectPath is otherwise stateless and safe to call concurrently -- a node builds more than one circuit at once -- so the Source I added this week introduced a race into an otherwise-clean Selector. Fixed with a mutex on last. TestSourceRaceUnderConcurrentSelect reproduces it. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THE DETECTOR'S OWN ABSENCE TAUGHT: 'race-clean' is only as true as the concurrency the tests exercise, and code that is never run concurrently under -race is not verified concurrent no matter how many times the suite is green. Both fixes verified, both race tests kept as permanent guards, and -race ./... over 24 axon+bootstrap packages is clean again including the two new tests. THE SWEEP WAS THEN EXTENDED TO THE OLDER CONCURRENT CODE, which carried 'race-clean' claims that -race had likewise never checked. Concurrency stress tests were added for the three highest-traffic shared structures and each was VERIFIED, not assumed: dht.Table (admit/query/sample/eject/sweep from 10 goroutines), peer.Peerbook (Observe writing while Sample/Get/Entries/Len read), and circuit.CircuitTable (admit/lookup/teardown/prune as a relay serves many circuits at once). All three are genuinely clean under -race. peer.Peerbook's cleanliness RESTS ON AN INVARIANT that was undocumented and is now pinned: Sample builds a slice of *PeerEntry POINTERS under the read lock and dereferences them AFTER releasing it, which is safe only because Observe REPLACES an entry with a fresh struct and nothing ever mutates one in place. A future in-place field update would silently make Sample race; a comment at the replacement point and TestPeerbookConcurrentAccess (which reads entry fields after Sample returns, under -race) now guard it. THE POINT STANDS REINFORCED: three older structures turned out to be genuinely concurrency-safe, but that was CONFIRMED by exercise rather than trusted from a claim -- and the two that were NOT safe were in code written the same week the detector started running, which is exactly where an unexercised claim was most likely to be false. |

The zero-loss clause of that half IS discharged -- it is enforced per cell, not reported. 4.4b RESOLVED 2026-08-21 BY SEPARATING TWO NUMBERS THE CRITERION CONFLATES. E5.2 reads 'a stated throughput floor', and the temptation was to adopt the measured 135 Mbit/s -- but 135 is an in-process UPPER BOUND on the crypto path, not a floor, and 5.1 already showed the SS8.6 window binds before the cipher at any RTT a 3-hop circuit sees, so a crypto-path number is not even the right floor for a DEPLOYMENT. So the throughput half is really TWO criteria. (1) A DEPLOYMENT SLA -- unstatable now, because it needs a network, an RTT and a target application; split out as 4.4c, blocked by 6.1 (no live traffic). (2) A CRYPTO-PATH NON-REGRESSION -- statable now, and what the in-process soak can honestly guard. TWO FLOORS STATED IN params WITH DERIVATIONS, both TRIPWIRES far below the measured 135 rather than targets, because a floor that fails on hardware variance teaches people to ignore failures. CircuitThroughputSmokeFloorMbps = 2.0 guards EVERY run including the 2-second default and runs under -race (~67x headroom, survives the race detector's ~10x slowdown plus a loaded CI runner; trips only on catastrophic breakage). CircuitThroughputRegressionFloorMbps = 20.0 guards the FULL 10-minute soak only (~6.75x headroom; the 10-min average is stable where a 2-second sample is not, and the soak is never run under -race). THE SOAK NOW ASSERTS INSTEAD OF ONLY REPORTING -- the same warn-versus-fail gap fixed repeatedly elsewhere -- and BOTH floors were verified by injection: raising the smoke floor above the measured rate fails the default run, and raising the regression floor fails a full-soak run (exercised with a temporarily shortened full-threshold rather than narrated, then reverted). Each constant carries the instruction: if it ever trips on hardware that is merely slow, LOWER it with a note, never delete the assertion. STILL OPEN as 4.4c: the deployment SLA, which is a real number a real network produces and not something derivable at a desk. 5.1 EVALUATED 2026-08-19: SS8.6's window figures were carried as unmeasured with none claimed, and they can now be EVALUATED because E5.2's soak measured the data path at 135.0 Mbit/s -- window and crypto finally sit on the same axis. A window of n cells permits at most n x 936 B / RTT. TWO THINGS FALL OUT AND NEITHER WAS WRITTEN DOWN. (1) THE CIRCUIT WINDOW IS EXACTLY 2x THE STREAM WINDOW IN BOTH CLASSES, so one stream can never use more than half its circuit and saturating a circuit needs at least two concurrent streams -- a deliberate ratio rather than a coincidence of two hand-picked pairs, and exactly the kind of relationship broken by tuning one number alone. (2) THE WINDOW BINDS BEFORE THE CRYPTO DOES at any RTT an anonymity network actually sees: against 135.0 Mbit/s, BULK's STREAM window is the bottleneck above roughly 110 ms RTT and INTERACTIVE's above roughly 10 ms, and a 3-hop circuit is not going to be under 110 ms. So on this hardware a bulk transfer is limited by SS8.6's window and not SS8.3's cipher, which means these figures are what a throughput complaint would be about. DOES NOT DISCHARGE P5b: the windows exist in PROSE ONLY -- no constant in internal/axon declares them and no flow-control loop consumes them, so there is nothing implemented to measure. What changed is that choosing them is now arithmetic against a measured ceiling rather than an open question. |

Live traffic still uses I2P. 2.11 PARTIAL 2026-08-19: internal/axon/dht/hsdir.go implements hsdir_index and the full position set, 8 tests. SS7 AND SS5 DISAGREE ON HOW MANY POSITIONS AND SS5 WINS. SS7.4 gives hsdir_index(j) for j IN {0,1} -- Tor's two-replica scheme -- and describes the result as 'two replica indices, each written to the DHT's r=8 closest holders, 16 holders'. But SS5 declares DescriptorReplicaPositions = 8 and says what it buys: 'with replica_index in the pre-image the 8 replicas sit at 8 unrelated keyspace points, so eclipsing a descriptor means eclipsing eight unrelated regions.' T7.5 states the criterion in SS5's terms -- 'publication reaches all 8 replica positions and a client fetching any 1 of 8 succeeds' -- so the code is written against 8 and SS7's j IN {0,1} is superseded. THE COST IS STATED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED: 8 publish lookups per period instead of 2, and at SS7's 8 KiB descriptor republished hourly that is 64 holders per period rather than 16; fetch is unchanged at one lookup because the client picks a single index. Period and SRV are both in the pre-image, tested: without the period a service's holders would be a stable enumerable set, which is the standing eclipse target rotation exists to deny, and without the SRV next period's mapping could be computed now and pre-positioned against. An out-of-range replica index is REFUSED rather than wrapped, because a wrapped index puts a descriptor where no client looks and presents as a service that is simply unreachable. PUBLISH LOOP BUILT 2026-08-20 (item 2.11): internal/axon/dht/publish.go, 11 tests. T7.5 HOLDS BOTH HALVES -- publication reaches all 8 positions with r=8 holders each and 8 DISTINCT keyspace points, and a client fetching EVERY index individually finds the record (trying one random index would have tested the property one eighth of the time). E7.3 HOLDS: time is swept across a full period and through the boundary at 17-minute steps, deliberately not an hour divisor, with the publisher republishing on its own hourly cadence rather than being nudged at the rollover, and the client resolving with ITS OWN clock at every step -- zero unreachable samples. THE PART THAT IS NOT A LOOP OVER ONE PERIOD: SS9.4 says 'period_len 86400 s; overlap 43200 s -> two periods valid at once', and the reason is that a client derives K_blind from its own clock, so a client slightly BEHIND is still in the previous period after a boundary and looks at eight positions the publisher has no reason to still write. For the first PeriodOverlap of every period the publisher therefore writes BOTH periods -- 16 positions, 128 holders at r=8, the same doubling SS9.4 states at its own superseded two-replica figure. Current period FIRST in the plan, so a publisher that is interrupted has written the positions everyone uses before the ones only a stale client does. A UNIT64 UNDERFLOW WAS AVAILABLE AT PERIOD 0 and is guarded: current-1 is 2^64-1, a blinded key for a period that cannot exist, asked for at the one moment nothing else would notice. PARTIAL PUBLICATION IS REPORTED, NOT SWALLOWED: every position is attempted even after one fails, because a publisher that stopped at the first error leaves the remaining positions holding the PREVIOUS descriptor -- so a client fetching one of those succeeds and gets stale intro points, presenting as a service that is up and BROKEN rather than one that is down, which is harder to diagnose. Reached() is one holder, not r=8: T7.5 asks that a position be reachable, and replication below r is a durability warning reported separately, or a thin routing table would present as a publication failure and hide the real one. Only VERIFIED contacts count toward a holder set (SS7.3 rule (c)), or a peer joins every descriptor's holder set by being mentioned in a FIND_NODE. The client picks its position at RANDOM and the rest as fallbacks in random order -- a client that always tried position 0 would make position 0's holders the only ones that matter, the standing target eight positions exist to deny, and would leave the other seven unobservably broken. TRANSPORT IS INJECTED as a StoreRPC func, the same shape Lookup's RPC already uses: the FIND_NODE/STORE wire over a circuit is item 2.10b, blocked by 5.2, and the publication SCHEDULE is testable without it. A REAL GAP FOUND AND PINNED RATHER THAN QUIETLY FIXED (item 2.11b): SS9.4's overlap is ONE-DIRECTIONAL. 'Two periods valid at once' means P-1 and P, which covers a client whose clock is BEHIND; a client whose clock is AHEAD, in the moments before a boundary, derives P+1 and NOBODY PUBLISHES P+1, so it finds nothing. Confirmed by test. Publishing P+1 as well would make three periods live and cost another 64 holders and is NOT what the specification says, so it was not done -- inventing it here would put the implementation ahead of the document with nothing recording why. TestFastClockFindsNothingJustBeforeABoundary asserts the GAP, so if the third period is ever added the test fails and the decision has to be made in the specification and the code together rather than silently in one of them. The exposure is bounded by clock skew, not by the overlap: a client d ahead has no descriptor for the d before each boundary. periodNumber is duplicated from internal/axon/identity rather than imported, to avoid a mutual dependency for one division, and a test asserts the two agree including at negative instants where both must refuse to wrap. D3 CHARACTERISED 2026-08-19 (5.2): internal/axon/session DOES NOT EXIST -- P23 is unstarted, not partly built. What it must provide is stronger than P23's own summary suggests. P23 describes 'a ratcheting session that survives circuit death', but T7.2 and E7.1 both demand continuity with NO BYTE LOSS AND NO DUPLICATION across a forced tunnel death, and a ratchet alone cannot deliver that: on migration a sender either re-sends what may already have arrived (duplication) or skips it (loss). THE REQUIREMENT IS ACKNOWLEDGED DELIVERY STATE THAT OUTLIVES THE CIRCUIT -- the session must know what the PEER has acknowledged, not merely what it sent, which is a per-session retransmit buffer and ack cursor, not a key schedule. Naming that now matters because Session{ID, SendChain, RecvChain, Step, Streams[]} as specified has nowhere to hold it. SECOND FINDING, THE SAME SHAPE AS E5.2's MISSING FLOOR: T7.2 requires the stream to continue 'within a STATED BOUND' and no bound is stated anywhere -- not in params, not in SS9, not in SS16 -- so the test is unwritable as specified even once the session layer exists. Logged as 5.2b. It also cannot be borrowed from E7.1, which says only 'zero application-visible error' and fixes no time. |

**`axon/13-threatmodel.md`**

| § | Section | Status | Notes |

| 18 | Threat Model | `PARTIAL` | Threat model written. 18.14 (supply chain) PARTLY CLOSED 2026-08-16: scripts/update-from-github.sh now verifies the commit it is about to build, fail-closed, with 4 tests against real git + ssh-keygen signatures. THE FINDING: there are TWO distribution paths needing DIFFERENT mechanisms, and the backlog item 'the updater must call release.Verify' was MIS-SPECIFIED. update-from-github.sh ships a COMMIT built locally as root, so it needs a COMMIT signature; internal/axon/release signs a MANIFEST over artifacts this path never downloads. The backend node_release.py path ships a binary and its sha256 IS NOT A SIGNATURE: it proves the object store returned bytes matching a digest THE SERVER ITSELF RECORDED in site_setting, so whoever compromises the server publishes any binary and every check passes. The verification policy is passed per-invocation with -c because gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile can be set in a repository's OWN config, and a mirror allowed to supply its own policy would be verifying itself; that is the fourth test. NOT ENFORCED YET: no commit on main is signed and no key is pinned, so every node takes the unpinned branch and prints a warning naming what is unprotected. Failing closed by default would brick every volunteer node on the next update. 2.2b DONE 2026-08-19: /api/v1/node/releases is now SIGNED. It publishes the sha256 of every node binary, and its docstring was careful about why that is separate from the download -- 'checking a file against a value that arrived in the same response proves only that they agree'. That defends against a tampered DOWNLOAD and does nothing against a tampered INDEX: an adversary who can answer for the origin simply publishes the hash of the binary they want trusted, and every check the client then performs succeeds. SS18.14 names the update channel as the strongest adversary against a real deployment, so this was the case that mattered most and it was unprotected. A SIGNATURE ALONE WOULD NOT HAVE BEEN ENOUGH: with no version inside the signed bytes it stops forgery and not REPLAY, so an older genuinely-signed index naming a binary whose flaw is now public still verifies. There was no timestamp or serial to use, so node_release gained a monotonic SETTING_RELEASES_SERIAL bumped by publish() IN THE SAME WRITE as the index it describes -- a separate write could leave a new index carrying an old serial, which careful clients would read as a replay and refuse. The signed bytes are the canonical JSON of `index` alone (sort_keys, compact separators), served under its own key so a client knows exactly which bytes were signed; signing the whole response would mean signing the signature, and signing only the hashes would let the platform-to-hash mapping be rearranged under a valid signature. When signing is unconfigured the field is ABSENT rather than null, because 'signature: null' reads as 'this one is fine unsigned' while a missing field lets a strict client fail closed. VERIFIED END TO END AGAINST THE LIVE SITE as a client would: the canonical bytes rebuild to the published hash, and the signature checks out against the public key at /.well-known/syndichan/origin-key.json. 6 tests, one injection. |

A tabletop produces an opinion about what the code would do; this produces the answer, and all four findings came from steps that failed to execute. FINDING 1, CONTAINMENT HAS NO MECHANISM in three of four structures: dht.Table has Admit and no counterpart, peer.Peerbook has Observe/Sample and no counterpart, and path.Selector takes Candidates func() []Relay so the pool is the CALLER'S and no component owns eviction. Only profile.Forget exists and it drops OBSERVATIONS, NOT MEMBERSHIP -- the relay is exactly as selectable afterwards, which is the trap. So containment today is: filter whatever supplies Selector.Candidates, then restart the node. Raised as 4.10b and 4.10c. 4.10b CLOSED 2026-08-20: internal/axon/contain, 10 tests, wired into dht.Table and peer.Peerbook with 9 more. REMOVAL ALONE WOULD HAVE BEEN THEATRE and that is the whole design: Admit re-inserts on the next FIND_NODE that mentions a peer and Observe re-creates the entry on the next probe, so an eject-only API would let a responder watch a relay walk straight back in while believing it contained. Containment is removal AND refusal, and both are tested by reproducing the theatre first (TestEjectWithoutDenyingIsTheatre, TestForgetWithoutDenyingIsTheatre). THREE RULES. (1) OPERATOR-SET, NEVER AUTOMATIC -- nothing may add an entry from observed behaviour, because treating churn as compromise ejects honest relays, which is a partition you performed on yourself and on a network of nine nodes is a partition that ends the network. Deny REFUSES without a reason, since six months on the only person who knows why a relay is contained is the one who typed it. (2) IT PERSISTS, and this is the point rather than a nicety: the procedure's containment step WAS 'restart the node', so an in-memory denial would have been erased by the very act prescribed to enforce it. Atomic temp+rename, and a file that exists but cannot be read is an ERROR rather than an empty list -- the failure mode being a node that quietly re-admits every relay an operator ejected. (3) BOUNDED BY REFUSAL, NOT EVICTION -- silently dropping the oldest denial to admit a new one would un-contain the first relay somebody worried about, and an unbounded list is a lever for an adversary who can induce denials to shrink a node's view until it is partitioned. Containment is checked FIRST in Admit, before the re-admission upgrade, or a contained relay keeps its slot by being mentioned once more; and BEFORE the quorum in Observe, because the quorum decides whether evidence is believable while containment decides whether this node will act on it at all. ErrContained is distinct from every cap and quorum error: those describe the NETWORK, this one describes a DECISION somebody made, and an operator debugging a thin table needs to tell them apart. SweepContained makes a denial retroactive; SetContainment deliberately does NOT sweep, so wiring a list in never silently reshapes a structure according to a list nobody has read. The drill is in check-claims.py's shipped set for a reason of its own: its record sheet is filled in DURING an exercise, which is exactly when somebody writes that no users were affected without a stated adversary. STILL NOT CLAIMED: the drill has not been run, and E16.4's human half stays open until the record sheet has real numbers in it. Rule: aggregate counts and THIS NODE'S OWN identity are allowed (a node signs its reports, so its id is attribution not surveillance); anything naming a THIRD PARTY or a UNIT OF WORK is refused -- circuit id, resolved name, object/shard id, another peer's identity, an address. Verified by injecting PeerID and CircuitID and watching it fail. IT FOUND A LEAK A SCHEMA RULE CANNOT SEE: Result.Detail is free text, passes every name check, and was assigned err.Error() from Go's HTTP client -- which reads 'dial tcp 203.0.113.9:443: connect: connection refused' and CARRIES THE RESOLVED ADDRESS OF THE TARGET. Now bounded at 200 bytes and IP-redacted, with the audit asserting EVERY assignment goes through the sanitiser rather than just the first. THE COMPANION GUARD WAS EXAMINING NOTHING, FOUND 2026-08-19 while closing 4.9b. It was written off as 'reports rather than fails', which understated it twice over. Its sender detector matched `http.(Post|NewRequest)(` and THIS TREE BUILDS 28 OF ITS SENDERS WITH `http.NewRequestWithContext(`, which does not match because of the trailing escaped paren -- so the walk found zero candidate packages and the test passed every run since it was written. Not a weak warning: a GREEN CHECK STANDING FOR AN AUDIT THAT NEVER RAN, which is worse than no check because it reads as coverage. FIXED THREE WAYS. (1) The detector now matches Post/PostForm/NewRequest/NewRequestWithContext. (2) TestEveryTransmitterIsAudited now FAILS rather than logs: every package that posts JSON must appear in EXACTLY ONE of `transmitting` or a new `notTelemetry` map that carries A WRITTEN REASON PER PACKAGE, and anything in neither fails naming both lists. The old reasoning -- 'not everything that posts is telemetry, a payment client posts too, so report rather than fail' -- was right about the premise and wrong about the conclusion: the fix for 'this needs judgement' is to REQUIRE the judgement, not to skip it. A stale exemption naming a package that no longer exists also fails, so a reason nobody re-reads cannot sit there forever. (3) TestTheDetectorIsNotVacuous is the guard on the guard: the detector must be able to SEE the packages already known to send telemetry, so the exact historical failure -- a regex that matches nothing -- cannot recur silently. Reverting the regex now fails loudly naming both monitor and heartbeat. ALL SEVEN UNCLASSIFIED PACKAGES WERE READ, NOT ASSUMED, and none turned out to be telemetry: channel and ethproof are JSON-RPC to chain endpoints, dcs is the local container API and does not leave the machine, facilitation posts signed PoF declarations that are attributable BY DESIGN, p2p posts lease requests and revocations to the coordinator, and directive is GET-ONLY -- caught anyway because the detector matches the request CONSTRUCTOR rather than the method, deliberately, since dcs passes its method in a variable and a method-based filter would miss a real sender. A SECOND BLIND SPOT FOUND AND PARTLY CLOSED: the schema audit parses STRUCT FIELD NAMES, so a payload built as map[string]any{...} is exempt by being unreadable to it. TestTransmittedPayloadsAreStructsNotMaps now refuses a marshalled map literal inside any AUDITED package. AND THE ONE REAL COST, STATED RATHER THAN EXEMPTED QUIETLY: internal/gateway's validator POSTs /api/v1/gateway/audit carrying `gateway` (another node's id) and `object_key` (a unit of work) -- both things T16.3 forbids in metrics -- AS A MAP LITERAL, so the schema audit could not have seen it even if the package were listed. It is classified notTelemetry because naming the subject is the FUNCTION of an accountability report, the same reasoning 89's report records rest on, NOT because the fields are harmless: an observer of that endpoint learns which gateway served which object. Raised as item 4.9c rather than silently blessed. 4.9c CLOSED 2026-08-20, AND THE PRIVACY CLAIM IN THE LINE ABOVE WAS OVERSTATED -- corrected here rather than left standing. Checked instead of assumed: `gateway` is an entry from the site's OWN published gateway directory and `object_key` is an entry from the site's OWN spot-check feed, defaulting to '/' -- the front page. Both ORIGINATE AT THE RECIPIENT, so posting them back tells it nothing it did not publish, and neither is a per-user, per-circuit or per-name identifier of the kind T16.3 exists to keep out of metrics. The earlier note that 'an observer of that endpoint learns which gateway served which object' was wrong on two counts: the endpoint is HTTPS to the origin, and the origin is the party that published both lists. THE STRUCTURAL DEFECT WAS REAL AND IS FIXED: the payload was a map literal, invisible to a schema audit that reads struct field names, so a field naming a genuine third party could have been added with nothing noticing. It is now a tagged struct with identical JSON keys -- the signature is over `message` and not over this encoding, and JSON key order is not significant, so the wire format the backend parses is unchanged. TWO GRANULARITY MISTAKES MADE AND CORRECTED WHILE CLOSING IT. First, the two field names were allowed GLOBALLY, which would have exempted `gateway` and `object_key` from the audit in monitor and heartbeat too, where they WOULD be a genuine third-party identifier; allowances are now PER SCOPE. Second, the whole package was added to `transmitting`, which dragged in the gateway REGISTRY protocol's types -- HostnameReservation, Address, directoryEntry -- things this node RECEIVES or registers about ITSELF, and exempting their fields to admit the package would have blunted the audit for exactly the names most worth catching. `transmitting` now accepts a FILE as well as a package, so internal/gateway stays classified as protocol traffic while validator.go alone is audited. Narrowing the scope was the correct direction; widening the allowances was not. Two injections verified: a PeerID field added to the audited file fails, and reverting the payload to a map literal fails. All three new guards verified BY INJECTION and reverted: an unclassified posting package, the old narrow regex, and a map-literal payload in an audited package each fail as intended. |

(1) WHO SETS DIFFICULTY: SS23.6 says the intro point publishes it, SS9.6 says the service does because only the service knows whether it is overloaded -- SS9.6 wins, since an intro point setting its own difficulty raises it under a flood the service is absorbing fine. (2) THE CONTROLLER: SS23.6 specifies +/-1 bit per 10s and calls it asymmetric rise-fast fall-slow, AND THAT PARAMETER CONTRADICTS ITS OWN RATIONALE -- +/-1 bit is x2 up and /2 down, symmetric in log space, permitting exactly the pulsing attack it warns about; SS9.6's x1.5+1 / x0.75 is genuinely asymmetric (+0.58 vs -0.42 bits) and is what SS23.6 meant. (3) THRESHOLD: SS23.6's depth>50 and SS9.6's q_target=6 are different queues; the controller runs on the service's, so 6 is operative. RisesFasterThanItFalls WAS WRONG IN EXACTLY THE WAY IT EXISTED TO CATCH: it compared LINEAR deltas, and for a multiplicative controller every step looks asymmetric that way (x2 from 1000 gains 1000, /2 loses 500), so it scored +/-1 bit as passing; now measured in log space. NO SCHEME IS CHOSEN and none is registered by default -- SS9.6 marks Equihash (n,k) NEEDS RESEARCH, and a package shipping hashcash as the default would pass every test here and be the failure SS9.6 names, targeted exclusion of exactly the users who most need the service; ReferenceHashcash reports MemoryHard false, New REFUSES it without AllowNonMemoryHardScheme (which exists to be greppable), and Verify with no scheme fails closed. PoWDifficulty IS DEFINED AS QUARTER BITS, its first definition: whole bits is too coarse, since the smallest change would be a DOUBLING, quantising the x1.5 rise and x0.75 fall to one step. T6a.3 MEASURED: solve 3.31ms, verify 2.0us, 1656x, so E6a.2's 1 percent bound holds with room -- but that measures THE DIAL, NOT MEMORY-HARDNESS. A TEST GAP FOUND BY INJECTION AND CLOSED: deleting the effort-dial check broke nothing, because effort is bound into the challenge so a forged claim dies one line earlier at the scheme check; the dial had no test until TestEffortDialIsWhatCostsTheClient. **`axon/29-governance.md`**

| § | Section | Status | Notes |

| 84 | The finding that shapes this Part: a relay cannot filter what it cannot see | `SPEC` | THE RULING THAT SHAPES PART X (R-84.1): policy applies at HOST, EXIT and PUBLISH -- the three positions where the node already knows what it is handling -- and NEVER at relay position. A relay that can filter by content category is a relay that can SEE the content category, which is the deanonymisation the whole of section 8 exists to prevent. Stated as permanent, not as a limitation to lift later. |
| 85 | Content identity — the layer everything else keys on | `SPEC` | Content identity keyed on section 12's on-chain NameRecord. R-85.1: a report names a manifest_cid (evidence must name what it is about) but accumulates against name_hash (or every report is voided by a republish). Unsolved: content legitimate at publication and abusive afterwards under an unchanged CID. G1 BUILT 2026-08-17: internal/axon/content, 6 tests. E-G1 HOLDS -- a report survives a content republish and still names the version it was made against. 11 FORCED A RULING 85 DID NOT ANTICIPATE: only a REGISTRABLE name has an on-chain namehash (NameHash() refuses a subordinate rather than inventing one), but 85 requires reports to accumulate against a name hash, so a subordinate would accumulate against nothing. R-85.2: a subordinate's reports count against its REGISTRABLE PARENT -- the chain is what governance can act on (93 can seize a registered name and has no handle on blog.acme.lab.axon), the registrant controls their own subordinates, and the alternative is a namespace where anyone sheds a report history by publishing under a fresh subdomain. ZoneID is computed over the name AS GIVEN so subordinates stay distinguishable within a shared subject. For() takes a name.Name and never a string, so ACME.LAB.AXON and acme.lab.axon cannot become two subjects. The owner is recorded PER OBSERVATION rather than resolved at read time, or R-93.3's retained seizure history would silently re-attribute every old report to whoever holds the name now. |
| 86 | Classification: labels, not verdicts | `SPEC` | 13 categories adopted. R-86.1: a label is an attributed, signed CLAIM, never a fact -- an unattributed label is a censorship primitive with no accountability, and reporter accuracy cannot be scored on anonymous claims. ILLEGAL/EXTREMIST/COPYRIGHT are jurisdictional and section 94 forbids global prunes on those grounds. G2 BUILT 2026-08-17: internal/axon/content/label.go, 7 tests. E-G2 HOLDS IN BOTH HALVES -- behaviourally an unattributed or unsigned label is refused, and by schema audit the Label type cannot express one. THE SCHEMA AUDIT WAS TOO WEAK ON FIRST WRITING: it counted func Sign( occurrences, so a second constructor named SignSkipped sailed past; found by adding one and watching it stay green. It now walks every top-level function returning a Label and requires an ed25519.Sign in the body (removing the Claimant field is caught by the compiler, which is stronger). The signature covers BOTH of 85s keys plus category and confidence, so a label cannot be moved to another name, re-pointed at another version, or recategorised with its signature intact. unknown is NOT SIGNABLE: it is the absence of a claim, and it is the zero value so an uninitialised Category is never a real claim. 94s rule is in the type: Jurisdictional() marks ILLEGAL/EXTREMIST/COPYRIGHT and PruneEligible() returns true for ONLY MALWARE and PHISHING. LabelSet does NOT reduce claims to a verdict and counts distinct CLAIMANTS separately from claim count, because 90s corroboration must be sublinear in identity count and conflating the two would defeat it before the weighting ran. |
| 87 | Node policy: what a node is willing to facilitate | `SPEC` | Node policy engine, HOST position only. R-87.1: the default for UNKNOWN is HOST, not refuse -- the proposal's 'unknown -> don't relay' inverts on a young network into 'store nothing' and makes labelling a gate on existence. Policy is local and never published: an advertised policy vector is a search index for whoever wants to seize a host. G3 BUILT 2026-08-17: internal/axon/content/policy.go, 8 tests. E-G3 HOLDS -- a node with host_block: malware refuses to store the object and RELAYS NORMALLY for every category. THERE IS NO RELAY-POSITION API AND THAT ABSENCE IS THE FEATURE: Position has no relay member so a relay decision is not expressible, and DecideRelay exists only to fail loudly at the call site somebody would reach for -- a package that simply omitted it would leave the next person to write their own filter, which is what R-84.1 forbids. R-87.1 IS THE ZERO VALUE: a fresh NodePolicy hosts unlabelled content, because the permissive default fails toward 'the network works' and the strict one toward 'the network is empty and nobody can tell why'. ONLY TRUSTED ISSUERS COUNT (R-88.1's local reducer one layer down): a stranger's signed malware claim is not false, it is not this node's evidence -- without that rule anyone could make any node drop any content by signing a claim about it. Block beats allow; an allow-list governs CLAIMS rather than absence. The policy is never serialised, by audit -- and that audit first matched the substring Publish inside PositionPublish, a legitimate R-84.1 position, so it now matches METHODS. |
| 88 | Reputation — and the collision with R14 | **`BUILT`** | COLLIDES WITH R14 AND IS RESOLVED. A network-wide reputation score is the global metric R14 forbids and P12a was built to avoid. R-88.1: reputation is a set of SIGNED ATTESTATIONS plus a LOCAL reducer -- no global score, no query returning one, first-hand observation always outranks attestation, and two nodes with different trusted issuers legitimately disagree. Decay is P12a's exponential form applied on read. G6/G7 BUILT 2026-08-20 (item 5.10): internal/axon/reputation, 14 tests. E-G6 HOLDS -- twenty trusted issuers all attesting the opposite of what the node measured do not move the value one bit, because a first-hand measurement is returned AS IS rather than blended; a weighted average would let enough issuers OUTVOTE a measurement, which is exactly the falsifier E-G6 names. Checked for all eight dimensions, since a single score would force the network to choose which of 'excellent reporter, poor governance participant' to be wrong about. E-G7 HOLDS IN BOTH HALVES: two reducers holding the SAME two attestations but disjoint trusted_issuers reach opposite conclusions, and the easily-skipped half -- both keep routing -- is enforced structurally, because the package offers NO predicate answering 'may I route through this'. That absence is the design: a reducer returning a boolean would be making the exclusion decision on the caller's behalf, network-wide by convention if not by protocol. TRUST IS APPLIED AT REDUCE TIME, NOT INGEST, so granting trust later makes what an issuer already said count without it repeating itself, and revoking it stops the count immediately -- refusing at ingest would make the trusted set a filter on HISTORY rather than on belief. Attestations are keyed by issuer LAST, so a second one about the same subject and dimension is a CORRECTION rather than a second voice (the same reasoning SS89's report keys rest on), and a stale one cannot overwrite a fresher one. A REAL DEFECT CAUGHT BY ITS OWN TEST: the reducer first returned a NORMALISED weighted mean, and a normalised mean NEVER DECAYS -- scaling every weight by the same factor cancels, so a single attestation from a year ago yields exactly the conclusion it did when fresh, while the value looks perfectly healthy. That is precisely T12a.5's failure, 'a score that only decays on write freezes when observation stops, and asserts a stale figure with undiminished confidence', reproduced in the code written to honour it. Fixed with the direct analogue of ProfileMinSamples: a floor on DECAYED weight below which the view returns to UNKNOWN, because Value alone cannot express staleness and Confidence has to. An aged-out view still reports Issuers and Weight, so 'what was said has aged out' is distinguishable from 'nobody ever spoke' -- the first is a reason to go find a fresher issuer. TWO PROVISIONAL PARAMETERS, stated with derivations per E14.3 and marked provisional because NOTHING MEASURES THEM AND NOTHING CAN YET -- nine nodes, no attestation ever issued, no distribution of issuer behaviour to fit. DefaultHalfLife is 7 days and deliberately NOT ProfileHalfLife's 1 hour: a profile metric measures a circuit that just happened, an attestation SUMMARISES a stated observation window and is a governance artefact, and ageing it out in an hour would mean none ever survives long enough to be worth issuing. DefaultMinWeight is 0.25, one lone issuer at two half-lives; ProfileMinSamples = 10 is explicitly NOT reusable, since attestations are orders of magnitude scarcer than circuit observations and a floor of 10 would mean none ever counted. NO BOOTSTRAP BY DECLARATION is enforced rather than described: a self-attestation is refused at SIGNING time, and an unattested subject is UNKNOWN with the value left at zero so a consumer must branch on Confidence rather than read it as neutral (R-87.1 makes UNKNOWN workable, not excluded). Issuer disagreement is REPORTED via AuditIssuer and never acted on -- SS88 puts the consequence locally with that node, and a reducer that quietly re-weighted its own inputs would make the resulting view unauditable, which is the same reason P3's peerbook records observations without scoring them. THE DEPLOYMENT CONSTRAINT IS A TEST, NOT A COMMENT: R-97.1 makes G6 deployable only after G17, because at nine nodes an attestation history identifies its operator completely (SS96) and 'a reading that treats reaching G6/G7 as permission to publish attestations is the privacy regression SS96 exists to prevent'. TestNothingHerePublishes fails if any file in the package acquires net/http, a DHT, link, circuit, tunnel or libp2p import -- a comment saying so does not fail. Raised as 5.10b so the ordering is on the list rather than only in a docstring. |
| 89 | The reporting protocol | `SPEC` | Reports are DHT records, not server submissions. R-89.1: evidence is content-addressed in the DCS, never a URL -- external evidence can be withdrawn after the vote. STATED COST: reporting is NOT anonymous, and a reporter in a jurisdiction where reporting is dangerous should not use it until section 96 exists. G4 BUILT 2026-08-17: internal/axon/dht/report.go, 6 tests -- a new DHT record class report alongside the six 7 defines. E-G4 HOLDS: three nodes decode the record, derive the key from THE RECORDS OWN FIELDS, check it against the key it arrived under and verify the signature, none having contacted the reporter. The key is subject-then-reporter and the ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: subject first so the neighbourhood is about the SUBJECT, reporter second so one identity filing repeatedly rewrites its own record instead of filling the neighbourhood with copies (a correction, not a second voice), while two reporters land on two keys or the second would overwrite the first. R-89.1 ENFORCED not documented: evidence that looks like a URL is refused at signing time, as is anything not exactly 32 bytes -- without that second rule evidence becomes a payload channel smuggled inside a governance record. The signature binds the evidence LIST order-sensitively, so reordering or TRIMMING THE INCONVENIENT HALF both invalidate the report. DELIBERATE NON-PROPERTY: the validator makes no moderation decisions -- a report naming an undefined category is still stored, because a validator that dropped reports it disagreed with would be moderating at the STORAGE layer where nobody can see it. |
| 90 | Reporter reputation and Sybil resistance | `SPEC` | R-90.1: no reporter can carry a prune alone at any reputation -- the cap is what stops convergence on a small number of trusted denouncers. Corroboration must be SUBLINEAR in identity count or k operator identities buy k-fold influence. Sybil resistance reuses P14 rather than inventing a second system, and inherits P14's [UNSOLVED] calibration in full. G5 BUILT 2026-08-17: internal/axon/content/reputation.go, 9 tests. E-G5 HOLDS -- one reporter at maximum reputation, flawless history and a proven bond cannot reach the prune threshold, and cannot get there by filing 50 times either. THE E-G5 TEST ASSERTS THE RELATIONSHIP NOT THE NUMBERS: weight < 1.0 would pass by coincidence after a recalibration that raised cap and threshold together, MaxSingleReporterWeight < PruneThreshold cannot. R-90.1 is what stops the system converging on a small number of trusted denouncers, the failure mode every reputation-weighted moderation system has actually exhibited. CORROBORATION MUST BE SUBLINEAR AND SS90's DRAFT DID NOT SAY SO -- under a linear factor k identities buy k times the influence, SS17's Sybil analysis applies unchanged and the weighting is decorative; sqrt is used, so doubling influence costs FOUR identities; log is so flat that fifty genuine reporters barely outweigh five. The exponent is provisional, the sublinearity is not. Corroboration scales the MEAN not the sum, or 200 zero-reputation identities outweigh one credible reporter. Independence is P12b's and peer.DomainKeys is NOT reimplemented -- it already carries the rule that an unknown domain yields NO KEY AT ALL so two unknowns never collide, and a second copy would drift the first time the ladder gained a rung; grouping is transitive union-find, so 20 identities under one on-chain operator are ONE VOICE. Unplaceable reporters count as their own group, which flatters, so Result.Undetermined reports how many. Accuracy is Laplace-smoothed. Every figure inherits P14's UNSOLVED calibration in full; the SHAPE does not. All four properties verified by injection. |
| 91 | Automatic categorization: confidence, never truth | NEEDS RESEARCH | R-91.1: a confidence estimate may inform a HOST decision (reversible, costs one node's storage) and may NEVER inform a prune (a censorship event with a governance record behind it). The two errors are not comparable so they do not get the same evidentiary standard. No corpus exists and the inputs are adversarial by construction. |

| 93 | The DAO as authoritative state oracle | `SPEC` | REVISED to the ORACLE model, then to SEIZURE BY KEY ROTATION. R-93.1: the CHAIN STATE is the oracle -- domainState/tldState are contract storage read through the ethproof light client, exactly as sybil.VerifyBond reads StakeVault; a signed statement is only ever a CACHE of already-authoritative chain state, threshold M-of-N or not built. R-93.2: an authoritative state transition, NOT a recommendation -- compliant nodes refuse resolve/publish/host-assign/DHT-advertise/market-list/registrar-transfer, RELAYING UNAFFECTED (R-84.1). PRUNED and SEIZED differ: seizure takes the NAME. R-93.4: THE DAO NEVER POSSESSES A DOMAIN KEY. Escrow refused permanently (one compromise impersonates EVERY domain, and M-of-N escrow is still escrow); disclosure refused (publishing a key hands it to everyone rather than disabling it); SEIZURE ROTATES domainKey TO ZERO and bumps version, so nobody can publish -- not the owner, not the DAO, not an attacker -- and no oracle key exists anywhere. AxonRegistry.sol ALREADY HAS THE FIELDS: domainKey, keyValidFrom, version, flags bit1 revoked. R-93.6: release() is immediate BY DESIGN and seizure must NOT share that path, or the seized party re-registers from a fresh wallet within a block. WHY ROTATION BEATS A FLAG: it converts compliance from POLICY into SIGNATURE VALIDITY -- a node that ignores the prune state still cannot resolve the name, because verifying a signature is not a policy setting. R-93.5 is the residual limit: a SNAPSHOT-COLD node enforces the last state it saw, so seizure is EVENTUALLY CONSISTENT at the speed of a node chain-sync -- unfixable, because a network able to push revocations to disconnected nodes has a push channel to every node, which is worse. R-93.3: recycling moves the name and never rewrites history; the quarantine before RECYCLABLE cannot be zero. THE BUG (4.21): the maniwani log shows a background thread 'media-s3-migration' dying every startup with 'RuntimeError: cannot exit context: thread state references a different context object' at shared.py's spawn_native_thread isolation wrapper (_ctx.run). It is BACKGROUND-ONLY -- zero request 5xx, container healthy -- so it is not user-facing, but it means the S3 media migration is not completing. THE OBVIOUS HYPOTHESIS WAS DISPROVEN BEFORE ANY EDIT: spawn_native_thread copies the context in the PARENT greenlet and runs it in the CHILD native thread, which looks like the cause, but a clean-interpreter reproduction of exactly that pattern (parent-copy, child-run, and even one shared context run across four threads) raises NOTHING. So the trigger is gevent-specific -- gevent.patch_all(contextvars=True) makes ContextVars greenlet-local and native threads are not greenlets -- and it cannot be reproduced or safely fixed without a gevent-monkey-patched harness. shared.py was therefore NOT edited on a hypothesis that had just been falsified: a wrong change to the Flask/gevent core breaks the whole site, and it is image-baked so it could not be hot-deployed or live-verified anyway. Recorded for a fix that reproduces under gevent first. NARROWED 2026-08-21 with FOUR reproduction harnesses under gevent.monkey.patch_all(contextvars=True) plus real Flask -- none reproduced the exact RuntimeError, which pins down what it is NOT and saves the next person the dead-ends. NOT the naive parent-copy/child-run pattern (clean). NOT simple gevent greenlet switches inside the copied context, single or many (clean). NOT a real Flask app_context() push/pop inside the copied context, even ACROSS a gevent.sleep switch (clean). NOT a nested copy_context with an unbalanced push (clean). A RELATED error IS reproducible and is the lead: resetting a contextvars Token created in the PARENT context from within the CHILD raises 'ValueError: Token ... was created in a different Context' -- same family as our RuntimeError, both being context/thread-state boundary mismatches. That points the finger at a token or app-context whose set and reset land on different sides of the copy boundary, in a way specific to the container's gevent and Python version (the repro box is Python 3.14, bleeding edge, where contextvars/gevent behave differently from a 3.11/3.12 container). SO THE BUG NEEDS THE ON-BOX STACK to reproduce -- the real gevent/Python versions, the real S3 client's contextvar usage, the actual migration loop -- and shared.py was correctly NOT patched, because a fix that cannot be reproduced cannot be validated and this is Flask/gevent CORE that breaks the whole site if wrong. THE CANDIDATE FIX DIRECTION, for validation where it reproduces: copy the context INSIDE the child thread (or run in a fresh one) so no token or app-context spans the spawn boundary -- but it must be confirmed against a live reproduction, not shipped on the strength of the diagnosis alone. WHY IT BROKE IS THE FINDING: every one of these stubs is guarded with `if X not in sys.modules`, so modules collected LATER do not install their own -- they PIGGYBACK on whichever module installed one first. The leak is therefore load-bearing for its dependants, and removing it correctly from the installer breaks the modules that were relying on it existing. That makes the remaining nine NOT independently fixable: a stub can only be restored once every module that piggybacks on it installs its own, so they have to be converted as a GROUP per stubbed module name, not one file at a time. The six that converted cleanly were the ones whose stub nobody else depended on. Analysing the import style of the module under test is necessary and NOT sufficient; the dependants have to be found too. 4.12 STOPPED AT 9 ON EVIDENCE, 2026-08-19. Restoring therefore does not merely remove a stub, it CHANGES WHICH MODULE'S STUB IS IN PLACE for everything collected later, and a dependant built against the richer one fails against the thinner. So the remaining nine cannot be converted file-by-file OR name-by-name; the stubs have to be made equivalent first -- one shared fixture with the union of what any module needs -- and only then can restoring be safe. R-93.3a ADDED 2026-08-19, resolving 5.7: the seizure quarantine length was NEEDS RESEARCH with only 'it cannot be zero' derived. More is available, and it does NOT come from the association-breaking argument the section rests on -- that bounds nothing, because a fresh wallet is unlinkable at any delay, so no quarantine length stops the seized party re-registering later; what it stops is the automated same-block re-grab, which needs only a few blocks. THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS THE APPEAL. An appeal is itself a governance proposal (SS94 puts appeal procedure in scope), costing one filing interval plus one full votingPeriod to decide. If the quarantine expires first the name reaches RECYCLABLE and the registrar may reassign it WHILE THE APPEAL IS STILL OPEN -- and once a third party holds it, a successful appeal cannot be honoured without taking the name from someone who did nothing wrong, so the seizure becomes irreversible by accident of timing, which is exactly what an appeal path exists to prevent. Hence SEIZE_QUARANTINE >= 2 x votingPeriod: one period to notice and file, one to vote. At AxonGovernance's 7-day default that is a 14-DAY FLOOR; descriptor propagation (SS7's 3 h) is three orders of magnitude smaller and does not bind. The deployed default of 30 days clears it at about 4.3x. THE MARGIN IS POLICY AND THE FLOOR IS NOT, so a test asserts the RELATIONSHIP between the two console defaults rather than pinning either number -- raising votingPeriod alone would walk into the reassign-during-appeal case and a test pinning 2592000 would not notice. Verified by injection: raising votingPeriod to 20 days fails it. ALL 11 CONTRACTS DEPLOYED TO ETHEREUM MAINNET 2026-08-21 (items 1.4-1.9), owner wallet 0xB2b3..64b6e; addresses recorded in memory and now in Go. THE GO NODE COULD NOT NAME THE CONTRACTS: the resolver/operator/sybil readers take an address through an injected seam (resolver.ChainSource, sybil.ProofSource, BondRef.Contract), which is correct, but nothing SUPPLIED the seam because nothing was deployed, and the addresses lived only in the backend's Postgres pof_contracts setting. internal/axon/contracts is the Go-side single source of truth -- one place, stated once, the same discipline SS11.3 applies to ROOT_SUFFIX -- so the wiring for 2.4/2.5/2.6 now has somewhere to read from. A TEST VALIDATES EVERY ADDRESS AS EIP-55, because a mis-typed nibble in a mainnet-money address is a payment sent nowhere and nothing else in the tree would catch it -- the readers take whatever address they are handed. Verified by injection: flipping one hex digit fails the test with the correct checksum shown. All 11 PoF addresses are valid EIP-55 as given (the Channels predecessor is recorded lowercase, as the console displays it -- a valid address, pre-rename ChannelManagerV2). DEPLOYED IS NOT WIRED, and the contracts package says so at the top: setTreasury+mintGenesis are unsent (supply is 0), setGovernor is unsent (AxonRegistry governance reverts NoGovernor), and the Epoch/StakeVault role wiring is unsent. Those are wallet transactions -- items 1.11/1.12/1.13 -- not code. A reader getting a zero bond from StakeVault or an ACTIVE-by-absence name from AxonRegistry is an HONEST answer about an unwired deployment, which is exactly why 2.7 (call AdmitStore) stays deploy-deep-blocked: wiring it now would refuse every writer, because no node has staked. |
| 94 | Governance scope: what the DAO may and may not decide | `PARTIAL` | R-94.1: the DAO governs the protocol and the network record, never nodes. VOTING WEIGHT IS DEFINED and the first draft was WRONG to call it unsolved: model/Dao.py SCORE_WEIGHTS is infrastructure 40 / reputation 30 / participation 20 / stake 10 -- a contribution-weighted hybrid in which stake is deliberately the SMALLEST term, so the wealthiest party does not decide what is suppressed. F-94.1 IS THE FINDING THAT MATTERS: only participation is measurable today (the other three report available=False), governance_score ends max(1, ...) so THE DEPLOYED SYSTEM IS ONE-MEMBER-ONE-VOTE, and THERE IS NO GOVERNANCE CONTRACT ON CHAIN -- DaoProposal/DaoVote are rows in the web server database and onchain_ref is nullable with the comment "Set once the Governance contract exists". That is load-bearing for 93: chain state authoritative + the vote in one server Postgres = a centralised oracle in a blockchain costume. SEQUENCING RULING: the Governance contract must be on chain BEFORE any PRUNED or SEIZED state is written. Also out of scope permanently: global prunes on ILLEGAL/EXTREMIST/COPYRIGHT grounds, which are jurisdictional and no vote resolves a conflict of laws. G8 WRITTEN 2026-08-18: contracts/AxonGovernance.sol, 16 tests, full contract suite 143 passing. F-94.1 said there is NO Governance contract on Ethereum and that DaoProposal/DaoVote are tables in one web server's Postgres -- load-bearing for 93, because if chain state is authoritative and the vote producing it is a row in one server's database then 'the blockchain is authoritative' means 'whatever that server writes is authoritative'. E-G8 IS THE DESIGN CONSTRAINT: every vote is a storage write and a tally is a pure read, verified by a test that rebuilds forWeight/againstWeight from raw storage with no events and no server. Weight is STORED AT VOTING TIME, not recomputed at tally time, or a source whose answer moves rewrites a tally with nobody voting. R-94.1 IS ENFORCED NOT DOCUMENTED: ILLEGAL, EXTREMIST and COPYRIGHT revert at PROPOSE time, so an out-of-scope proposal never exists to be voted on -- refusing at execution instead would let a majority record a passed vote to suppress content on jurisdictional grounds and leave the refusal looking like a technicality. F-94.1 IS ENFORCED TOO AND THIS IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART: only participation is measurable, so the deployed weighting is one-member-one-vote, the Sybil-bait case 94 warned about. A governance contract that shipped anyway WITH POWER TO SEIZE NAMES would look correct and be trivially captured. So a REGISTRY ACTION requires live weight sources covering at least minCoverageBps of SCORE_WEIGHTS, and the CONSTRUCTOR REFUSES any floor at or below 2000 -- W_PARTICIPATION alone is 2000 bps -- the same move as AxonRegistry's ZeroQuarantine refusal, for the same reason: a deployment carrying it would look correct. A participation-only DAO can therefore VOTE and cannot PRUNE, and that is tested both ways. SIGNAL proposals execute regardless, since they change no state. A REVERTING weight source is read as DARK rather than as everyone-scores-zero, because the latter silently moves the denominator and changes every tally. Weight NORMALISES BY LIVE WEIGHT not by W_TOTAL: dividing by 100 with three sources dark scales everybody down alike, changes no outcome, and makes a partial scheme look like a full one. SCORE_WEIGHTS are on chain as constants (40/30/20/10) with a test that stake stays the smallest term. finalise() is permissionless, since requiring a privileged call to notice a deadline would let inaction hold a proposal open indefinitely. NOT DEPLOYED: needs 1.4 (AxonToken) first, and after deploying somebody must call AxonRegistry.setGovernor(). The console now offers it (12 contracts live). |
| 95 | The economic layer | `SPEC` | Host and relay offers. R-95.1: a relay offer is priced by BYTES and carries no category field, because a relay has no category to price. Reputation affects RANKING, never eligibility -- exclusion-by-default is the bootstrap problem and it reduces to pay-to-enter. Depends on placement.Candidate.Domains, which is built and NOT POPULATED BY ANY CALLER (OUTSTANDING E1). G11 BUILT 2026-08-17: internal/placement/reputation.go, 7 tests. R-92.2 HOLDS -- a host with a perfect record that shares a failure domain with an existing holder is refused, and the slot goes to an UNKNOWN host in a distinct domain. THE FIRST VERSION WAS A SILENT NO-OP AND EVERY SET-BASED TEST PASSED IT: PlanWithReputation ranked candidates and called Plan, which applies its own emptiest-first sort and overrode the ranking whenever FreeBytes differed. Comparing WHICH hosts were selectable cannot detect that, because the selectable set is exactly what reputation must not change; it was caught only by a test asserting reputation DOES reorder. The gate is now extracted into planOrdered, which tries candidates in the order given, and Plan and PlanWithReputation each sort then share that one copy of the constraint. REPUTATION IS NEVER AN ADMISSION TEST -- not a floor, not a threshold. It cannot widen (R-92.2) and must not narrow either: a floor makes dispersal FAIL where nobody has a history yet (R-87.1s shape at the storage layer), and it would STARVE NEW HOSTS PERMANENTLY, since a host with no history can never earn one if it is never selected -- a reputation system that cannot onboard is a cartel with extra steps. Unknown is the NEUTRAL PRIOR not last, reusing G5s Laplace 0.5, and Observed is a separate field because scored-0 and never-seen are different facts. Scores bucket to one decimal place because raw float comparison makes 0.71 beat 0.70 at a precision the attestation counts do not have. Scores are LOCAL (R-88.1); a global host score would be the measurement authority R14 forbids. An audit asserts no second copy of the domain gate. Three injections verified. |
| 96 | Privacy-preserving reputation | NEEDS RESEARCH | Prove a reputation threshold without revealing activity. NOT v1, and the ordering matters: deploying section 88 without this, at 9 nodes, publishes each operator's complete hosting and relaying history, which at that scale IS the operator's identity. Deploying reputation now is a PRIVACY REGRESSION. |
| 97 | Phases G1–G20 | `SPEC` | Phases G1-G20 with exit criteria. Build order DIFFERS from the proposal's: node reputation (G6) and privacy-preserving proofs (G17) are transposed relative to Phases 3 and 19, because of section 96. G12 (path reinforcement) and G13 (multipath) are ALREADY BUILT -- P12a and Part VI. Order: G1-G4, G8-G10, G18, G14, G5, G11, G6/G7, G15, G16, G17. R-97.1 ADDED 2026-08-19 (5.11): SS97 CONTAINED A LIVE CIRCULAR DEPENDENCY. Its table gives G17 depends on G6; its build order puts G6/G7 before G17; and the justification one line later says node reputation 'waits for either SS96 or a population large enough' -- and SS96 IS G17. So G6 waits for G17 while G17 waits for G6. The 'or' was the intended escape and IT IS CLOSED TODAY: the deployed population is nine nodes (PAR-15), the exact scale SS96 names as one where 'that history identifies the operator completely'. The cycle is live, not hypothetical, and anyone following SS97 literally stalls. BROKEN BY DISTINGUISHING TWO KINDS OF DEPENDENCY: G17's need for G6 is a SCHEMA dependency -- proving 'I have sufficient reputation in category X' requires the attestation format and category vocabulary to be fixed, not for any reputation to have accumulated. G6's need for G17 is a DEPLOYMENT dependency -- the schema can exist and be tested with synthetic attestations; what must not happen at nine nodes is publishing real ones. So G17 IS BUILDABLE FIRST against G6's schema and G6 IS DEPLOYABLE ONLY AFTER G17. The build order stands; what changes is that reaching G6/G7 means IMPLEMENTED AND TESTED, not PUBLISHED -- and reading it as permission to publish attestations is precisely the privacy regression SS96 exists to prevent. OUTSTANDING corrected in both directions: 5.11 unblocked, 5.10 no longer blocked by it but carrying the deploy-after condition. |

## Fixed defects

Bugs found and fixed while deploying. Listed because each is a class of failure
worth not repeating.

| Defect | Where | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway-controller hijacked the apex A record | `gateway-controller/config.yaml` | `public_hostname` pointed at gateways, so 2 of 3 requests to the apex missed the web server. |
| Heartbeat upsert race | `model/StorageNode.py` | Concurrent beacons both INSERTed; loser 503'd forever. A healthy node could be permanently invisible. |
| Presence endpoint hardcoded | `internal/heartbeat`, `cmd/…/main.go` | Nodes beaconed the old domain; failure was logged and retried, never fatal. |
| 503 handler swallowed its traceback | `blueprints/storage_nodes.py` | Heartbeats failed continuously and invisibly from both ends. |
| Peers endpoint used the admin map helper | `blueprints/storage_nodes.py` | Filtered to geolocated nodes and would have exposed `last_ip`. |
| Static sync re-uploaded everything each boot | `model/Media.py` | ~6 min blocking startup → every deploy a multi-minute outage. Now incremental (9s). |
| `internal-error.html` deleted with the strip | `backend/templates` | Every 500 became a TemplateNotFound *inside the error handler*, hiding real causes. |
| `bootstrap.py` stamps alembic at head after `create_all()` | `backend/bootstrap.py` | Models not imported at that moment get tables no migration will ever create (broke PoF). **Not yet fixed.** |
| nginx `upstream` cached a dead container IP | `deploy-configs/nginx.conf` | 502s after every rebuild until nginx restarted. Now resolves per-request. |
| Cell padding was a covert channel | `internal/axon/link/cell.go` | Decoder ignored bytes after the declared payload, so every relay would forward attacker-chosen data hidden in the padding. **Found by FuzzDecode**, not by review. |
| Head-of-line test measured the wrong thing | `internal/axon/link/link_test.go` | Kept circuit A writing at full rate, so B slowed from **bandwidth contention** and the test called it head-of-line blocking. Flaky at every threshold (baseline varied 2.2–13.3 ms). Now stalls A idle and asserts **liveness**, not a ratio. |

## Phase ledger — complete vs partial

Updated by hand. The tables above are generated per SECTION; this is per PHASE,
because a section can read `BUILT` while the phase that built it still has
criteria outstanding, and that difference is exactly what gets lost.

### Complete — every stated criterion discharged

| Phase | Evidence |
|---|---|
| **P0** Architecture & threat model | Constitution R1–R14 / C15–C21 govern every later section; adversary model frozen. |
| **P1** Cryptographic identities | `internal/axon/identity`, 23 tests. T1.1–T1.5, E1.1, E1.2. Includes scalar-arithmetic verification of Ed25519 blinding. |
| **P3** Peer discovery, reachability, NAT | `internal/axon/peer`, 44 tests. T3.1–T3.5, E3.1–E3.3. E3.1 = 10⁴ `Sample(20, distinct-/24 ∧ distinct-ASN)` draws, zero violations. |
| **P5a** Non-malleable cell construction | `internal/axon/circuit/wideblock.go`. T5a.1–T5a.5, E5a.1–E5a.3. E5a.1 = **0 cross-hop channel hits over 10⁶ cells**. Closes PAR-01. |

### Partial — built, with named criteria outstanding

| Phase | Built | Outstanding |
|---|---|---|
| **P2** Secure transport | `internal/axon/link`. T2.1–T2.5, E2.1, E2.3, E2.4. E2.1 = 10⁶ cells/transport, identical digest. | **E2.2** ("within 10 %") needs a controlled link with stable RTT, not a loopback pair — the test asserts the qualitative R12 property instead. **T2.6** (two independent builds emit identical QUIC Initials) needs a reproducible-build harness that does not exist. |

Size favours the VOPRF and decides nothing; T2 decides it. T1–T4, the client-side minimum age, T15.1/T15.2/T15.3/T15.5, E15.2. **E15.1 is empirical** — `removability_test.sh` deletes the package, builds the module and runs every data-path suite, and was verified to fail when a dependency is injected. | `blindrsa.go` is classical **RSA-FDH; production must be RFC 9474** (PSS), a different encoding with different issuer-side checks. **There is no epoch key schedule**, and the epoch length is the denominator of the anonymity set. **T15.4** (aggregator golden vectors) and **E15.3** (M6 demonstrated) need the settlement path and a network. And §14.3's own arithmetic is why none of this is in v1: the set is at most `P·B`, dominated by `P`, and the deployed population is **9 nodes with zero paying clients**. |

### Not started

13 of the 16 parity phases (§23.4, §23.6) — everything except P5a, P12a and
P12b. **Every phase P0–P16 of the original plan has now been started**; what
remains of them is enumerated by blocker in [OUTSTANDING.md](OUTSTANDING.md). Parts V–VIII of the roadmap (sections 26–75) are the
research programme and later layers and are unstarted by design.

### Standing caveats that no phase closes

1. **PAR-15 — the population gap.** 9 nodes, none carrying anonymous traffic,
   zero external review. Not closable by building. It bounds every claim above.
2. **Live traffic still uses I2P.** The deployed site does not route over any of
   this. §9 and §22 say so.
3. **`bootstrap.py` stamps alembic at head after `create_all()`**, so models not
   imported at that moment get tables no migration will ever create. **Still not
   fixed.**
4. **The three adversarial review passes** over Parts I–VIII were commissioned
   once and never ran. PAR-01 — a defect in the layer everything rests on, found
   by writing one test — is a fair estimate of what a real review would surface.

## Next

1. **P7 — anonymous services and tunnel pools** (§9.2–9.4): what turns M2's
   one-shot rendezvous into a service that stays reachable. Carries PAR-05
   (bounded sampled guard set) and PAR-10 (pre-built pool spares).
2. **P6a — the intro puzzle** (PAR-16, `critical`). Blocked on choosing
   Equihash-style parameters defensibly, which needs measurement on real
   hardware including the low-power end.
3. **P7a — vanguards** (PAR-04): the highest-severity mechanism gap for the
   thing this network exists to host.
4. Fix `bootstrap.py`'s alembic stamping so fresh databases get every table.
5. The three adversarial review passes over Parts I–VIII.
